heading: Selected Engineering Challenges
subtitle: Case studies from consulting work across regulated, security-sensitive and enterprise domains.

studies.title: Centralized Transaction & Certification Platform
studies.summaryQuote: Designing transaction flows where correctness matters more than convenience.
studies.contextNote: A simplified architecture, based on patterns from enterprise financial and certification systems (drawn from work on a centralized application for ANCERT, Spain). Details are generalized on purpose, to protect client confidentiality.
studies.problem: A national certification authority had many manual, paper-based processes spread across different teams. They needed one centralized application — without breaking the workflows those teams already relied on.

responsibilities: Authenticates and authorizes the caller
Validates request shape before it reaches business logic
Applies rate limiting
Coordinates the transaction lifecycle
Enforces business rules
Maintains state transitions
Handles retries and failures
Checks business rules before any state changes
Rejects malformed or fraudulent requests
Maintains the authoritative balance and transaction history
Enforces double-entry accounting invariants
Deduplicates retried requests using an idempotency key
Returns the original result instead of reprocessing
Persists transaction state within ACID boundaries
Isolates concurrent writes to the same account
Publishes a durable record of what happened
Decouples the transaction path from downstream consumers
Builds a tamper-evident trail for compliance and dispute resolution
Informs the client and internal teams of the outcome
Reconciles with the external payment provider

decisions.question: Why a centralized transaction service instead of letting each module write to the database directly?
decisions.answer: Sending every state change through one place made it easy to enforce consistency rules and auditing in a single spot — instead of repeating (and slowly breaking) that logic in every module.

decisions.question: Why idempotency as its own concern instead of relying on clients not to retry?
decisions.answer: Retries happen at scale, no matter what: network timeouts, double-clicks, dropped connections. An idempotency key per request meant a retried transaction just returned the original result, instead of creating a duplicate.

decisions.question: Why an event stream alongside the synchronous path to the database?
decisions.answer: The transaction itself needed a fast, consistent write. But audit, notification and settlement could happen a bit later. Using events for those kept the main path fast, and let each of them fail on its own without blocking the rest.

decisions.question: What happens when an external settlement provider fails?
decisions.answer: The transaction is already saved before settlement is attempted. So if the provider fails, the system retries with a delay, then falls back to a compensating flow and reconciliation. The ledger is never left in an unclear state.

studies.title: Document Signing Workflow
studies.summaryQuote: Long-running workflows where every step needs to be provably correct.
studies.contextNote: Drawn from work in the certification and digital-signature domain (ANCERT, Spain). Details are generalized to protect client confidentiality.
studies.problem: A document needed to go through identity checks, get signed, and stay fully auditable. If a user dropped off mid-way, the process couldn't lose its place — and it couldn't cut corners on cryptographic security just for convenience.

responsibilities: Confirms the signer is who they claim to be before any signature is collected
Re-verifies the signer at the moment of signing, not just at session start
Applies a cryptographic signature bound to the exact document content
Runs under an idempotency key so a retried request can't produce a second signature
Appends every step as an immutable, timestamped record
Reconstructs the full history for legal disputes

decisions.question: Why make every step idempotent instead of relying on the client to avoid duplicate requests?
decisions.answer: Network retries and double-clicks happen all the time at scale. An idempotency key per step meant a retried request just got back the same result, instead of creating a second, conflicting signature.

decisions.question: Why keep the audit trail as an append-only log instead of updating a status field?
decisions.answer: Legal audits need to show exactly what happened and when — not just the current state. An append-only trail keeps that full history, even if a later step corrects an earlier one.

studies.title: Identity & Wallet Authentication
studies.summaryQuote: Letting users authenticate with a wallet without reinventing identity management.
studies.contextNote: A representative architecture drawn from identity and authentication work across several consulting projects, generalized to protect client confidentiality.
studies.problem: An application needed to support login with a crypto wallet, alongside normal login. It couldn't build a custom identity system from scratch, and it couldn't cut corners on standard protocols.

responsibilities: Issues and validates OAuth2 / OIDC tokens
Delegates wallet signature verification to a custom authentication flow
Manages session and token lifecycle for every downstream service
Trusts a single token format regardless of how the user logged in
Never handles raw credentials or private keys
Signs a challenge to prove ownership of the private key
Returns the signature for Keycloak to verify

decisions.question: Why Keycloak instead of a hand-rolled identity provider?
decisions.answer: Identity looks simple but has many tricky details: token lifecycles, revocation, standards compliance. Keycloak is a proven OIDC provider, so the team could add a custom wallet login flow on top of it — instead of building and maintaining all of that from scratch.

decisions.question: Why treat wallet auth as another Keycloak authentication flow instead of a parallel system?
decisions.answer: Keeping wallet login inside the same identity provider meant every other service still trusted one token format and one session model — no matter how the user proved who they were.
